title: Spending the budget, and what is still refused for its own reason once it is gone

expect.why: The first of the flood is answered on its merits — the session is in open mode, so there is no lease to take. That is the baseline the refusal further down is measured against, and it is why this scenario never moves the session out of open mode: no lease is ever granted, so it leaves nothing behind for the next client.

Thirty acquires against a budget of five a second: the budget goes, and the limiter answers. Asserted of *some* repetition rather than a named one, because which repetition first finds the budget gone is a fact about the clock, not the contract. The bucket refills a token every two hundred milliseconds, so a flood alternates — a thirty-deep run reads 409 409 409 409 409 429 429 ... 429 409, the final 409 being a token handed back mid-flood. This used to be pinned at the eighth repetition on the reasoning that eight requests take tens of milliseconds, so at most one token could have returned by then. On a loaded runner they take longer, another token returns, and the eighth is answered on its merits — the scenario then failed for being fast enough to matter, having asserted how quick the machine was rather than what the server owes.

The refusal names the reason and nothing else — no budget, no window, no Retry-After. A caller told when to come back would also be told the shape of the limit. This holds of the same repetition as the status and the flag above, not of some other one: a 429 in one repetition and the word `rate_limited` in another would be a weaker claim wearing this one's clothes.

The client library's own reading of a 429. A library that treated an unfamiliar refusal as success would leave its caller believing the request landed — and, for a flood, believing it holds a lease it was never granted.

Authorization runs before the limiter, so a worker that does not exist is still absent rather than rate limited even with the budget gone. A 429 here would answer a question the caller was not entitled to ask: whether the worker exists.
And in the `detail` envelope, byte for byte the same refusal an unspent budget gives — the rate limit must not change what a refusal says, only whether the request got that far.

Authentication runs before the limiter too. An unauthenticated caller is told it is nobody even when the budget is gone; were it told 429 instead, a flood would become a way of learning that the worker is there.

Two envelopes in one scenario, deliberately: the rate limit answers in `error` and authentication in `detail`. A client has to know both, and a port that picked one for everything would pass every other scenario in this directory.

The budget is the lease routes', not the server's. Reading the session list still works with the acquire budget spent — a limiter that took the whole API down with it would turn one impatient client into an outage.
